youtube.title: Your Toast Isn't Unlucky, Your Table Is #Shorts
youtube.description:
Omar's toast keeps landing butter side down. It's not bad luck.

Toast sliding off a table pivots on the edge and starts to spin. From a normal table (about 75 cm) it only has time for about half a turn, so the buttered top ends up on the floor. Physicist Robert Matthews worked this out in 1995 and won the 1996 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics for it. For a full turn you would need a table about 3 metres tall. In 2001, British schoolchildren dropped toast almost 10,000 times: 62% landed butter side down. Matthews' fix: give the falling toast a smart swipe forward so it barely rotates.

Would you buy a taller table, or just learn to swipe?

Sources:
- Matthews (1995), Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants, European Journal of Physics 16(4): https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995EJPh...16..172M/abstract
- Paper summary and full text: https://www.fermatslibrary.com/s/tumbling-toast-murphy-s-law-and-i-i-the-fundamental-constants
- NPR (2001), Buttered toast: https://www.npr.org/2001/03/09/1119717/buttered-toast
- Ig Nobel 1996: https://improbable.com/airchives/miniair/twentieth-century/MINI9610

Omar, Lena and the cafe are fictional.
